evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: can you just give me a sense of what the treatment center landscape looks like? Is it highly fragmented? Are there a few... I'm just trying to figure out where can you go and get people in large bunches?

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: Because my concern is that this is a really great idea, and I'm struggling to understand how you're going to get the product in front of enough people to actually make the business side work.

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: Yeah. I guess I just worry that if treatment centers are small and fragmented and they're hard to find and sell, you might have the world's greatest product but a really difficult time…

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: I think you've been super thoughtful about the needs of your customer and how this can extend beyond the time that they spend in treatment.

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: My one concern though is for all of the attention and time that's been invested in the product and the product experience, I worry maybe not enough time has been spent thinking about the go to market and sales strategy.

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: And what it's going to take I think ... I totally believe the long term arc I just worry though, you need a bridge to get to that end state.

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles

rationales.explanation: Charles asks how fragmented the treatment-center landscape is and where the company can access customers in sufficiently large groups.
He explicitly struggles to understand how the product will reach enough treatment-center users for the business to work.
Charles worries that small, fragmented, hard-to-find treatment centers will make customer acquisition and selling difficult.
Charles positively characterizes the founder as thoughtful about customer needs and the product's broader use.
He recognizes customer-centered product thinking and extending the solution beyond treatment as strengths.
Charles's central concern is that insufficient attention has been given to go-to-market, sales strategy, and an economically workable treatment-center acquisition model.
He identifies the missing bridge as a clear, economically viable way to acquire treatment centers and develop a sales strategy.
Charles states that he believes in the company's long-term arc, while distinguishing that belief from concern about the near-term bridge.
He affirms that the founder is spending time and attention appropriately during the pilot stage.

Charles directly ties his decision to the absence of a clearly defined, remotely cost-efficient strategy for acquiring the first ten and hundred clinics, and says he would revisit after greater market clarity.
He questions whether the customer-acquisition model can make the business work and concludes that the business is not yet right for him.
The decision is conditioned on gaining clarity about how the company will attack the treatment-center market and acquire its initial clinics.

annotation_summary: Charles's Out decision is explicitly driven by insufficient clarity on a scalable, cost-efficient go-to-market and treatment-center acquisition strategy. He positively endorses the product's customer focus and long-term direction, but does not view the current market-entry bridge as sufficiently defined.
